questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a relation from a function by testing whether any input repeats with a different output
questions.stem: A snack machine maps each keypad entry to the item it drops, but the entry labelled 4 delivers either crisps or chocolate depending on which slot was filled last. Which statement about this mapping is correct?

options.text: It is a relation but not a function, because the input 4 has two different outputs

options.misconception: believes any rule that always gives some output is a function

options.text: It is neither a relation nor a function, because the two possible items cannot be ordered
options.misconception: thinks a relation must have its outputs in a fixed order to exist

options.text: It is a function on the keypad but not a function on the slot numbers used inside
options.misconception: assumes changing the label of the input repairs a repeated input

questions.explanation: A relation is any pairing of inputs with outputs, so this keypad rule is a relation. A function must send each single input to exactly one output, and the input 4 breaks that rule whenever the two slots hold different items. The trap is the feeling that 'pressing 4 always drops something' is enough, but the second condition is about uniqueness, not existence, and a rule that returns two different items for one key fails it.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the single input 4, and whether its output can ever differ.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain why a strictly increasing linear rule has an inverse function
questions.stem: Explain why the function f of x equal 3x minus 5 has an inverse function, and state the rule that inverse follows.

answer.exemplar: The rule 3x minus 5 is strictly increasing, because each output is reached by exactly one input: whenever two inputs gave the same output, subtracting 5 and dividing by 3 would force those inputs to be equal as well. A function like this is one-to-one, and a one-to-one function can be reversed, which is what having an inverse means. To find it, write y equal to 3x minus 5, exchange the letters x and y to get x equal to 3y minus 5, and then solve for y, which gives y equal to the quantity x plus 5 divided by 3. That last rule undoes the original: taking a value, adding 5 and dividing by 3 recovers the input that produced it.

questions.explanation: An inverse function exists precisely when each output came from exactly one input, because reversing the pairing is only possible if there is nothing ambiguous to reverse. The rule 3x minus 5 is one-to-one since the operations it applies cannot send two different inputs to the same output, so the reversal is well defined. The construction is then forced: swap the roles of input and output, and solve for the old input, which here gives the quantity x plus 5 divided by 3.
questions.hint: Think about whether any output can be traced back to two different inputs.

Write the original rule with y standing for the output and x for the input

Exchange the two letters so that each plays the part the other played

questions.explanation: The first step fixes the notation, since an inverse is described by the same pairing read backwards, and only after x and y have their roles can those roles be exchanged. Solving for the old input next produces an actual rule rather than a rearranged sentence, and the final check guards against a plausible looking but wrong reversal, which is easy to produce by careless algebra. Skipping the swap gives back the original rule, and solving before swapping gives an equation that still has y on both sides.
questions.hint: Nothing can be exchanged until the letters have been assigned their roles.

options.text: The rule 2 times x squared, minus 5 times x
options.misconception: keeps an even power that stays put while the input is negated

options.text: The rule negative 4 times x, plus 9
options.misconception: believes a linear rule is automatically odd regardless of its constant

questions.explanation: An odd rule must have no even powers and no constant term, so that negating the input negates the whole value. In 2x cubed minus 5 times x both terms are odd powers, and the rule passes the test: the input 2 gives 6, and the input negative 2 gives negative 6. The other three each smuggle in something that stays put under negation, and one surviving even term is enough to destroy the property.
questions.hint: Odd means the entire value changes sign, so nothing may stay behind.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: use the horizontal line test to decide whether a function is one-to-one
questions.stem: A graph passes the vertical line test, so it is a function, yet a single horizontal line cuts the graph in three places. What does that second fact tell you?

The graph is not a function, since a horizontal line meets it more than once
options.misconception: switches to the wrong test and forgets the vertical one passed

options.text: The function has an inverse function, and the inverse passes the vertical test
options.misconception: believes passing the vertical test is enough to guarantee an inverse

options.text: The function is one-to-one, and only its drawing style is unusual here
options.misconception: reads a graph feature as a cosmetic difference rather than a real one

questions.explanation: One output with several inputs is the horizontal line failure, and it means the rule is not one-to-one, so reversing the pairing would be ambiguous and no inverse function exists. Passing the vertical line test settles only that the graph is a function; it says nothing about reversing. The trap is treating the two tests as interchangeable, since one asks about inputs and the other about outputs.
questions.hint: The horizontal test is about outputs, and an inverse needs every output to be unique.

options.text: It is the same curve as the original, since the rule was not changed
options.misconception: believes an inverse leaves every plotted point where it was

options.text: It is the mirror image of the original graph across the vertical y axis
options.misconception: negates the input on its own instead of exchanging the two roles

questions.explanation: Reversing a function swaps the input and output of every point on its graph, and the set of points obtained that way is the mirror image across the line y equals x, since that line is the set of points whose two coordinates are equal. Reflecting across an axis would negate one coordinate while leaving the other, which is not a reversal of the pairing. The most common wrong answer is the claim that nothing changes, which would only hold if the graph were already symmetric about that line.
questions.hint: Ask where each plotted point would have to move to reverse the pairing.

Each band was located by testing the input against its stated condition rather than by proximity to a boundary, which is the move a step function forces. Pricing 5 hours in the middle band by rounding downwards would give 12 instead.

3, reached where the input turns negative on the left of 2

options.misconception: takes the value at a nearby input as though it were the minimum

options.text: 7, obtained by treating the plus 5 as though it were added to the input
options.misconception: misplaces the vertical shift inside the absolute value argument

Both neighbouring inputs confirm the point: at 1 and at 3 the rule gives 8, which is larger. 5, because 9 minus 4 is the result of the first branch at that input
options.misconception: tests the condition wrongly and uses the branch for smaller inputs

options.text: 4, because the boundary input of 2 is squared to give that value
options.misconception: substitutes the boundary instead of the input that was asked for

options.text: 7, because the two branch values averaged at 3 give that figure
options.misconception: believes the branches blend into one value between their regions

The first branch would have produced 5, which is the value at an input where it does not apply, and squaring the boundary would answer a different question altogether. Averaging branch values has no meaning, since a piecewise rule is selected rather than blended.

2x plus 7, the same rule with the two letters exchanged

options.misconception: divides the input by the slope instead of dividing the whole rule

The 7 must be subtracted, since undoing a shift of 7 in the output means moving back 7, and then the whole result is divided by 2 to undo the scaling. Exchanging the letters and stopping leaves the original rule, which reverses nothing.

The inequality points the wrong way, and the true domain is x at most 5 thirds
options.misconception: reverses the inequality while dividing by a positive coefficient

options.text: The constant is handled wrongly, and the true domain is every x greater than 8
options.misconception: combines the two terms in the radicand instead of subtracting them

options.misconception: imports the shape of a denominator restriction onto a square root

The strict version throws away one legal input for no reason, and the other options each substitute a familiar but wrong pattern: a reversed inequality, an arithmetic combination error, or a denominator rule applied to a root.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain why a composition can have a smaller domain than its inner function
questions.stem: Explain, with a worked example, why the domain of the composition of f with g can be a smaller set than the domain of g alone.

answer.exemplar: The input to the outer function in a composition is not the original input, it is the output of the inner function, so the outer rule's own restrictions have to be checked against the range of g rather than against the set of allowed inputs. Take f of x equal to 1 divided by the quantity x minus 2, whose domain is every real number except 2, and g of x equal to 4 minus x, which is defined for every real number. The inner rule always produces a value, but the composition fails exactly when that value equals 2, which happens when 4 minus x equals 2, that is at x equals 2. So the domain of the composition is the domain of g with one input removed, and writing the composition out as 1 divided by the quantity 2 minus x shows the same removal directly.

questions.explanation: A composition passes values along a chain, and each link applies its own restrictions to what the previous link produced, so restricting one stage removes inputs from the whole chain. A rule only has to be legal where it is actually used, which is why the inner rule can be perfectly well defined on an input whose output then breaks the outer rule. Writing the composition as a single rule makes the same restriction visible without any talk of ranges.
questions.hint: Ask which value the outer function receives, rather than which value it started with.

options.text: For each input that repeats, collect every output written beside it
Accept the table as a function only if each repeated input has one single output
Otherwise record the rule as a relation with an ambiguous input and output
Scan the input column for any value that is written down more than once

questions.explanation: The scan has to come first, because the whole test concerns inputs that appear more than once, and gathering the outputs beside a repeated input is the evidence the test needs. Only then can the verdict be read off, and the verdict is about that single property rather than about the table as a whole. Deciding before collecting the evidence means guessing, which is how a table with a shared output gets wrongly rejected.
questions.hint: Nothing can be collected until the repeated inputs have been found.

Set the radicand below zero and record that inputs must be at least 2
Write the domain as every input from 2 upwards with 5 cut out of it
Check one input from each surviving piece to confirm the rule is defined

The domain then falls out as the inputs that satisfy both at once, which here is every real number from 2 upwards with 5 removed. Testing a point from each surviving piece is the last step and a real safeguard, because it catches a combination written down from memory rather than from the two conditions.
questions.hint: Find the two restrictions first, keep only what satisfies both, then test it.

questions.topic: Composition domain against an inner range

The range of g is wider than the domain of f, so the two sets cannot be used
options.misconception: measures the two sets against each other in the wrong direction

options.text: The claim holds, since f and g are each defined wherever they are entered
options.misconception: checks each rule at its own input and ignores the chain between them

options.text: Only inputs where g is undefined are lost, and g is defined for every real
options.misconception: looks for the restriction in the inner rule's own domain rather than the chain

questions.explanation: In a composition the value handed to the outer rule is produced by the inner one, so the inputs that survive are those where g's output lands inside f's domain. Here every value g produces is below negative 1 while f accepts only inputs from 0 to 10, so the two sets never meet and the composition has an empty domain. This is why neither rule being defined on the reals says anything about the composition, and why the claim cannot be rescued by widening anything.

options.misconception: multiplies the two rule values where a reduction was requested

Subtracting the other way round produces a different rule, and that is the most common error here because the arithmetic is otherwise identical. Adding instead would be the sum of the two functions, and multiplying would be their product, both of which answer a different question.
questions.hint: Keep the order the question gives: first rule reduced by second.

x equals negative 2 and negative 3, from factoring with both signs turned

Each sign in that factorisation has to match the sign in the rule, which is why the both-negative version is a common slip. Substituting settles it: 4 minus 10 plus 6 is zero at the input 2, and 9 minus 15 plus 6 is zero at the input 3.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Smallest input allowed by a composition

questions.stem: Let f of x equal the square root of x, and let g of x equal 2x minus 9. What is the smallest whole number that belongs to the domain of the composition of f with g? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The composition sends the input through g first, so the quantity that must be zero or positive is 2x minus 9 rather than the input itself. Solving gives x at least 4.5, whose least whole number is 5, and the boundary check makes the rounding concrete: at the input 5 the inner rule gives 1, which has a real square root, while at the input 4 it gives negative 1, which does not. Reading the radicand as the bare input would wrongly allow 0.
questions.hint: The radicand is the value the inner rule produces, not the original input.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Using evenness to evaluate a rule
questions.learningObjective: use the even property to find the values of a rule at an input and its negative
questions.stem: The rule e of x equal to 3x squared minus 5 is even, so its values at 4 and negative 4 agree. What is the sum of those two values? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Evenness says the value at a negated input equals the value at the input, so it is enough to compute one of them: 3 times 16 minus 5 is 48 minus 5, which is 43, and the sum of the two equal values is 43 doubled, which is 86. The same figure appears by computing the second value directly, since squaring negative 4 gives 16 as well. Treating evenness as though it produced opposite signs would instead subtract, and that is the odd property rather than the even one.
questions.hint: Compute the value once, then double it, since the two values are equal.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Using oddness to evaluate a rule
questions.learningObjective: use the odd property to find the value of a rule at a negative input
questions.stem: The rule o of x equal to 2x cubed minus x is odd. What is the value of o at the input negative 3? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Oddness means the value at a negated input is the negative of the value at the input, so computing the positive side is enough: 2 times 27 minus 3 is 54 minus 3, which is 51, and the value at negative 3 is negative 51. Substituting directly confirms it, since cubing negative 3 gives negative 27, giving negative 54 plus 3, which is negative 51. Dropping the sign because the rule is odd, or doubling instead of negating, both answer a different property.
questions.hint: Compute the value at positive 3, then change the sign and nothing else.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: translate a charging rule stated in words into a computation
questions.stem: A taxi charges a fixed 4 dollars plus 1.50 dollars for every kilometre travelled, and an airport surcharge of 2 dollars is added to the fare. What is the total charge for a journey of 8 kilometres? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The rule in words is c of k equal to 4 plus 1.5 times k, so at 8 kilometres the distance charge is 1.5 times 8, which is 12, and adding the fixed 4 dollars gives 16, and the 2 dollar surcharge then brings the total to 18. The same total comes from collecting the money in a different order: 12 plus 2 is 14, and 14 plus 4 is 18. Forgetting the fixed charge, or taking the surcharge off before multiplying, are the two slips that produce other figures.
questions.hint: Separate the distance charge, the fixed charge and the surcharge, then add them.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Domain and zero of a rational rule
questions.learningObjective: state the domain and the zero of a fractional rule and reject a cancellation
questions.stem: A rule is f of x equal to the quantity 2x minus 8 divided by x minus 2. Which statement about its domain and its zero is correct?

options.text: The domain omits 2, and the only zero is 4, which is not the omitted input
The domain omits 4, because the numerator vanishes there and the value is zero
options.misconception: takes the input that gives a zero to be the input that is excluded

options.text: The domain omits both 2 and 4, since a zero numerator also halts the rule
options.misconception: excludes a zero numerator as though it were a zero denominator

options.text: The domain omits 2, and cancelling a common factor then makes the rule equal 2
options.misconception: cancels first and loses the excluded input in the process

questions.explanation: Only the denominator restricts the domain, so the input 2 is omitted, while the zero comes from the numerator, and 2x minus 8 vanishes at the input 4, which is perfectly legal. The factorisation 2 times the quantity x minus 4 over the quantity x minus 2 has no common factor to cancel, so the rule does not simplify to a constant and option D describes an impossible step. Confusing the numerator's zero with the denominator's zero is the most common way to mis-state a domain like this one.
questions.hint: Find the zero of the denominator and of the numerator separately, then compare them.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Domain of a composition with a root
questions.learningObjective: find the domain of a composition whose inner rule feeds a square root
questions.stem: Let f of x equal the square root of 4 minus x, and let g of x equal x squared plus 1. Which set is the domain of the composition of f with g?

options.text: From negative root 3 up to root 3, since the radicand becomes 3 minus x squared
Every input up to 4, by using the domain of the outer rule on its own
options.misconception: ignores that the inner rule changes the quantity under the root

options.text: Every real number, since squaring the input keeps the quantity below 4
options.misconception: assumes the inner rule can never push the radicand negative

options.text: From 4 upwards, by reading the radicand as x minus 4 and inverting it
options.misconception: reads the radicand with the wrong sign and flips the inequality

questions.explanation: Substituting the inner rule into the outer one gives the square root of 4 minus the quantity x squared plus 1, which is the square root of 3 minus x squared. That radicand must be zero or positive, so x squared must be at most 3, giving every input from negative root 3 to root 3, and both endpoints are allowed because the radicand is zero there. Using the outer rule's own domain would let in every input up to 4, which fails as soon as x squared passes 3.
questions.hint: Write the composition as one rule first, then require its radicand to be zero or more.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Inverse found by flipping a sign
questions.learningObjective: correct an inverse that changes only the sign of the constant term
questions.stem: Asked for the inverse of f of x equal to 3x minus 8, a student writes f inverse of x equal to 3x plus 8 and argues that reversing a rule only means undoing the shift. What is the error?

options.text: The whole result must be divided by 3, giving the quantity x plus 8 over 3
The 8 must be subtracted before dividing, giving the quantity x minus 8 over 3
options.misconception: keeps the sign of the constant when undoing a shift of 8 downwards

options.text: The result must be multiplied by 3, giving 3 times the quantity x plus 8
options.misconception: inverts a multiplication by scaling up instead of dividing

options.text: The rule already reverses itself, so no division is needed at any point
options.misconception: assumes a rule with a slope is its own inverse function

questions.explanation: Reversing a rule means undoing every step it performs, and a rule of 3x minus 8 scales by 3 and then shifts down by 8, so the reversal shifts up by 8 and then divides by 3, giving the quantity x plus 8 over 3. Changing only the sign leaves a rule that scales by 3 again, which cannot undo anything, and the round trip proves it: 3 times 2 minus 8 is negative 2, while 3 times negative 2 plus 8 is 2, so the two do not undo each other. Dividing by 3 at the end is the step the student dropped.
questions.hint: Undo each operation the rule performs, in the opposite order, including the scaling.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: A domain with a root and a denominator
questions.learningObjective: correct a domain claim that ignores the restriction under a square root
questions.stem: For the rule v of x equal to the square root of x minus 1, all divided by x minus 4, a student claims the domain is every real number except 4. What is wrong with that claim?

options.text: The quantity under the root must be zero or positive, so inputs below 1 are out
The root condition is the only one that matters, so the input 4 stays allowed
options.misconception: drops the denominator restriction once the root is examined

options.text: Both conditions hold for every real input except 4, so the claim holds
options.misconception: believes a square root accepts any input at all, so no radicand test exists

options.text: The root condition must be positive rather than zero or more, so 1 is out
options.misconception: insists on a strict inequality and wrongly removes the boundary input

questions.explanation: A rule with a root above the fraction bar still has to satisfy the root's own condition, and the quantity x minus 1 is negative for every input below 1, so those inputs are outside the domain. The true domain is every input from 1 upwards with 4 cut out of it, because the boundary 1 is allowed and 4 is not. The student's claim keeps the one restriction that is easiest to see and drops the one that lives inside the root, which is where restrictions are most often overlooked.
questions.hint: Every subexpression has to make sense, not only the one below the fraction bar.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain what makes a graph a step function and how to tell it from slanted pieces
questions.stem: Explain what makes a graph the graph of a step function, and how you can tell such a graph apart from one built out of slanted pieces.

answer.exemplar: A step function takes one fixed value across a whole interval of inputs and then jumps to a different value at a stated boundary, so its graph consists of flat pieces joined by vertical jumps rather than by sloping lines. Take a rule that gives 4 dollars for a stay under 2 hours, 6 dollars from 2 up to 5 hours, and 9 dollars for 5 hours or more: the output is 4 across one whole interval, 6 across the next, and 9 after that, which is a step shape. A function made of slanted pieces behaves differently inside each piece, because a small move in the input produces a corresponding change in the output instead of no change at all, as a rule of x for the first five hours and 10 minus x afterwards would show. The practical test is therefore to move the input around inside a single piece and ask whether the output budges at all: if it stays exactly the same, that piece is a step, and if it rises or falls, the piece is slanted.

questions.explanation: The defining feature is that the output is constant over an interval of inputs, so a horizontal stretch of graph with nothing on it but a jump at the end is what a step function looks like. A piecewise linear function can share the same boundaries and the same starting and ending values, so the boundaries alone never settle the question. Sliding the input along one piece and watching whether the output moves distinguishes the two immediately, since only a slanted piece responds.
questions.hint: Hold the input inside one piece and ask whether the output changes at all.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain why a function failing the horizontal line test has no inverse
questions.stem: Explain why a function whose graph fails the horizontal line test cannot have an inverse function, and use a concrete example to make the reason clear.

answer.exemplar: The horizontal line test asks whether some single output is reached by two different inputs, and if that happens the reversal is impossible, because an inverse function would have to send that one output back to two inputs at once. Take the rule f of x equal to x squared on the whole set of real inputs: the value 4 is produced by the input 2 and also by the input negative 2, so the question what input gave 4 has no single answer to record. Since a function may give only one output for each of its inputs, the reversed pairing cannot be written as a function at all, which is why an inverse is said not to exist. The same formula restricted to the inputs of 0 and above would be one-to-one and would have an inverse, so the obstruction is the repeated output rather than the rule itself.

questions.explanation: Reversing a pairing only works when the reversal is a pairing in its own right, and a repeated output breaks that because one output would then need two inputs. The graph makes it visible: a horizontal line meeting the curve twice is a single height reached from two different directions along the graph. Restricting the domain until the clash disappears is the repair, which also shows the property belongs to the domain as much as to the rule.
questions.hint: Ask what would have to happen to the repeated output if the pairing were reversed.
